claims.claim: Averaged over the planet, about 340 watts per square meter of solar energy arrives at the top of Earth's atmosphere; roughly 29 percent is reflected back to space and about 71 percent is absorbed by the Earth system (about 23 percent in the atmosphere and about 48 percent at the surface).

The natural greenhouse effect — greenhouse gases absorbing outgoing thermal infrared and re-radiating some of it downward — keeps Earth's average surface temperature near 15 degrees Celsius, more than 30 degrees warmer than it would be without an atmosphere.
The ocean covers more than 70 percent of Earth's surface and holds about 97 percent of Earth's water (about 1.34 billion cubic kilometers of a total of about 1.39 billion).

Unequal solar heating between the equator and the poles drives three atmospheric circulation cells per hemisphere (Hadley, Ferrel, Polar) and ocean currents that carry warm water away from the equator and cold water back from the poles; together this coupled atmosphere-ocean circulation is called Earth's heat engine.
The water cycle moves water among ocean, atmosphere, land, and groundwater through evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and runoff, driven by solar energy and gravity.

Evaporation from tropical oceans, and the release of latent heat when the vapor condenses, are primary drivers of the atmospheric heat engine; evaporation also removes about 25 percent of incoming solar energy from the surface.

El Niño and La Niña are the warm and cool phases of ENSO, a natural oscillation of the tropical Pacific that swings every 3-7 years; weaker trade winds during El Niño leave the central and eastern tropical Pacific warmer than average, stronger trade winds during La Niña leave it cooler, and the shifts move rainfall and modify jet streams worldwide.
ENSO neither adds nor removes heat from the climate system as a whole; it shifts heat back and forth between the ocean and the atmosphere.

The atmosphere and oceans behave as one coupled system whose components exchange energy and water continuously; the ocean's large heat capacity makes it a slow, steady partner that stores and gradually releases heat.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Share of Earth's water held in the ocean.
positions: NOAA Ocean Service: 'About 97 percent of Earth's water is in the ocean.'
USGS Water Science School: 'Oceans store 96% of all water on Earth.'
Arithmetic on NOAA's own volumes (1,335,000,000 of 1,386,000,000 cubic kilometers) gives about 96.3 percent.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states 'about 97 percent' with NOAA's figures and gives the volumes; the discrepancy is rounding of the same underlying estimate. Noted in the USGS source record.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Fraction of Earth's surface covered by water.
positions: NOAA Ocean Service: 'The ocean covers more than 70 percent of the surface of our planet.'
USGS Water Science School: water in liquid and frozen form 'covers 75% of the Earth's surface' (counting ice cover).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses NOAA's 'more than 70 percent' for ocean coverage specifically, which is the standard figure; the higher USGS value counts frozen water too. The evidence packet records both.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Earth's effective temperature without the greenhouse effect.
positions: NASA Earth Observatory energy budget article: effective temperature viewed from space is about -20 degrees Celsius, and the greenhouse effect makes the surface 'more than 30 degrees' warmer.
Other NASA educational pages commonly cite about -18 degrees Celsius for the no-greenhouse average.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson avoids the exact no-atmosphere temperature and uses the article's own robust phrasing: surface near 15 degrees Celsius, more than 30 degrees warmer than without an atmosphere.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Exact reflection/absorption split of incoming solar energy.
positions: NASA Earth Observatory (2009 article, updated 2025): 29 percent reflected, 71 percent absorbed (23 atmosphere, 48 surface).
Older textbook estimates often round to 30/70.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the NASA article's about-29/about-71 figures with 'about' qualifiers and notes in the source record that energy-budget values are estimates with uncertainty.

correctionsNeeded: No prior machine-generated draft existed for this topic in content/phase-3 (no phase-3 lessons.json store found); the content-progress entry was a 'planned' placeholder. All lesson content was written fresh and verified against sources.
The 70 percent ocean-surface figure was checked against NOAA (more than 70 percent) and used instead of the USGS 75 percent figure, which counts frozen water as well.

sourceRecords.title: Climate and Earth's Energy Budget
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NASA). Read live with a browser user agent (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21; article dated January 14, 2009, last updated September 18, 2025. Primary support for: ~340 W/m2 global average insolation at the top of the atmosphere (and ~1,360 W/m2 total solar irradiance on a directly facing surface); ~29 percent reflected / ~71 percent absorbed (23 percent atmosphere, 48 percent surface); surface energy loss via evaporation (25 percent), convection (5 percent), and net thermal infrared (17 percent); the natural greenhouse effect raising average surface temperature to about 15 degrees Celsius, more than 30 degrees warmer than without an atmosphere; coupled atmosphere-ocean circulation as Earth's heat engine; evaporation from tropical oceans and latent-heat release as primary drivers of the atmospheric heat engine; and the ocean's heat capacity giving the climate thermal inertia. Energy-budget values are presented in the article as estimates with uncertainty. Facts synthesized; no wording, figures, or diagrams reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: How much water is in the ocean?
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA). Read live with a browser user agent (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21 (page last updated 06/16/24). Supports: the ocean covers more than 70 percent of Earth's surface; about 97 percent of Earth's water is in the ocean; total Earth water about 1,386,000,000 cubic kilometers and ocean water about 1,335,000,000 cubic kilometers. Arithmetic cross-checked in python3: 1,335/1,386 = about 96.3 percent, consistent with the 'about 97 percent' rounding. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What is a current?
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA). Read live with a browser user agent (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21 (page last updated 06/16/24). Supports: ocean currents are driven by wind, water density differences, and tides; currents affect climate by carrying warm water from the equator and cold water from the poles; the Gulf Stream example of milder winter weather in Bergen, Norway than in New York. Used only for the brief heat-transport passage; deep ocean circulation mechanics belong to the ocean-circulation sibling topic. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: El Niño and La Niña: Frequently asked questions
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA). Climate.gov is an archived site as of June 25, 2025 (current NOAA climate resources live at www.noaa.gov/climate), but the page returned its full content when fetched with a browser user agent on 2026-08-21; the canonical climate.gov URL is registered. Reviewed by NOAA CPC forecasters (Halpert, Barnston, L'Heureux, Becker). Supports: El Niño and La Niña as the warm and cool phases of ENSO; swings every 3-7 years on average; weaker- or stronger-than-average easterly trade winds initiating each phase; warmer-than-average central/eastern tropical Pacific and eastward rainfall shift during El Niño (and the reverse during La Niña); modification of jet streams and weather patterns worldwide; and the statement that ENSO does not add or remove heat from the climate system but shifts it between ocean and atmosphere. ENSO-specific U.S. winter impacts kept general; no attribution claims made. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Global Atmospheric Circulations
sourceRecords.provider: NOAA National Weather Service, JetStream Online School for Weather
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA/NWS). Read live on 2026-08-21. The legacy weather.gov/jetstream URLs now redirect to a JetStream hub on noaa.gov; the current page for this content is the registered URL (linked from https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream/global-weather). Supports: unequal solar heating between the equator and poles produces global circulations of air and heat, and each hemisphere contains three circulation cells — the Hadley cell (low latitudes), the Ferrel cell (mid-latitudes), and the Polar cell (high latitudes). Used only to name the cells briefly; cell mechanics, weather, and jet-stream topics are sibling topics. Facts synthesized; no wording or diagrams reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Water Cycle
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Geological Survey, Water Science School
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (USGS). Read live with a browser user agent (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. Supports: the water cycle as where water is on Earth and how it moves; oceans storing 96 percent of Earth's water (USGS rounding; NOAA says about 97 percent — see conflictingEvidence); energy from the Sun and the force of gravity driving the cycle; evaporation and evapotranspiration moving water from land and ocean into the atmosphere; condensation forming clouds; precipitation returning water to the surface; and runoff, streamflow, infiltration, and groundwater recharge moving water across and below the surface. Used only for the cycle itself; groundwater and surface-water detail belong to sibling topics. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
